notes.heading: Account for the measuring instrument and the source
paragraphs: Ideal circuit rules simplify both the power supply and the instruments. An ideal voltmeter has infinite resistance and draws no current; a real finite-resistance meter can change the circuit it measures. An ideal battery maintains its stated voltage, while a model with internal resistance has a terminal voltage that decreases as current increases. Always state which model is being used before applying a familiar divider rule. Energy conservation requires that the power supplied equals power transferred in all resistive elements, including any internal resistance included in the model.

questions.prompt: A model battery has emf 12 V and internal resistance 1 Ω. It supplies a 5 Ω resistor. Find current, terminal voltage and power in the external resistor.
questions.answer: Current 2 A, terminal voltage 10 V, external power 20 W.
solution: Use total series resistance 6 Ω to obtain 12/6=2 A.
The external drop is 2×5=10 V and its power is I²R=20 W.

questions.prompt: Two 10 kΩ resistors form a divider across an ideal 12 V supply. A 10 kΩ voltmeter is placed across the lower resistor. Find the indicated voltage and compare it with the unloaded value.
questions.answer: The meter reads 4 V; the unloaded value is 6 V.
solution: The lower resistor and meter combine in parallel to give 5 kΩ.

questions.prompt: An ideal 9 V supply feeds 3 Ω and 6 Ω resistors in parallel. Find each branch current and verify total power using both VI and the sum of branch powers.
questions.answer: Currents are 3 A and 1.5 A. Total power is 9×4.5=40.5 W, also 27+13.5 W.
solution: Each parallel branch has 9 V; divide by its resistance.
Sum branch currents or branch powers and compare the totals.
markingPoints: Compute total power 40.5 W from VI.
Verify branch powers sum to 40.5 W.
